title: Tephritid Microbe Functions
text:
Tephritid flies host specialized microbial partners that play vital roles in their physiology and ecology.

These symbionts contribute to nutrient acquisition, digestion, and development—helping their hosts thrive across a range of environments.

Below are key examples of functionally important microbial associations identified in major Tephritid species:





Nitrogen metabolism

Obligate symbiont Ca. Erwinia dacicola

Accelerated larval development
(Campos et al., 2022)






Enhanced development and longevity

Carbon and nitrogen metabolism

Suppression of pathogenic Pseudomonas
(Behar et al., 2008)






Facultative symbiosis with Enterobacter and Klebsiella

Purine degradation

Nitrogen provisioning
(Ren et al., 2022)

title: Tephritid Microbe Functions
text:
SIT × Microbiota

The Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) is a powerful, environmentally friendly method for pest control that relies on the mass release of sterilised males to suppress wild populations through infertile matings.

However, irradiation and mass-rearing conditions can disrupt the natural gut microbiota of flies—potentially reducing male fitness, competitiveness, and lifespan.
Microbiota restoration through probitoics could enhance SIT effectiveness.
By supplementing or reintroducing beneficial bacteria (e.g., Klebsiella, Enterobacter, or genera of the Enterobacteriacae family), it may be possible to:
Improve sterile male mating competitiveness

Increase survival and flight ability post-irradiation

Support nutrient assimilation and energy metabolism during stress

Reduce handling stress and mortality during release

This shows the importance of “SIT × Microbiota” in using the microbiota for pest management; optimising the sterile insect performance.

title: Microbial Sequencing of Flies
text:
A fly’s microbiota can be sequenced using several approaches, including:

Short-read 16S rRNA sequencing
Long-read 16S rRNA sequencing
Shotgun metagenomic sequencing

Short-read 16S rRNA sequencing:

Targets and sequences short variable regions of the 16S rRNA gene (e.g., V3–V4) -
Uses sequencing platforms such as Illumina. - It provides high-throughput, cost-effective profiling of bacterial community composition but limited taxonomic resolution, often to the genus level.

Long-read 16S rRNA sequencing:

Sequences the full-length 16S rRNA gene using technologies like Oxford Nanopore or PacBio.
This approach improves taxonomic resolution, often enabling species- or even strain-level identification, though with higher cost and potential sequencing error rates.
A problem with some Medfly papers is that despite use of long-read sequencing, some results only show to the genus level, this is due to a lack of update in taxonomic classifiers.

Shotgun metagenomic sequencing:

Sequences all genomic DNA present in a sample, not just the 16S rRNA gene.
It allows for comprehensive profiling of microbial diversity (including bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses) and provides insights into functional gene content, metabolic pathways, and strain-level variation.

Sequencing of the Medfly gut microbiota:

The majority of Medfly sequencing studies use short-read 16S, there are only a few to have used long read sequencing.
This year, Mason et al. 2025 have published two studies that have sequenced the Medfly microbiota, however their results only go to the genus level.
There have been no studies in Medfly, or even Tephritids, to have used metagenomics.
We plan to do a pilot metagenomic study: with a small sample size to establish if we get any microbial DNA, or to see if Medfly DNA overrides this.

title: Tephritids
text:
For this round, there will be a soft introduction to Tephritds. One of the most beautiful insect families to exist.

The family Tephritidae includes over 5,000 described species worldwide.
These are the “true fruit flies” unlike with Drosophilidae like Drosophila melanogaster, apparently known as the “fake fruit flies”.
Female Tephritids possess a well-developed ovipositor used to puncture fruit and deposit eggs beneath the skin.
Species are a mix of monophagous, and polyphagous.
Not all are pests, but the map below demonstrates distribution of some of the Tephritid pests.








As you might be able to tell, these pests are distributed in the warmer countries.
